parole.significato: one-eighth of a Mexican real (issued until 1897)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tlaco (“half”).
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tlahtlaōyoh.
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tlālcoyōtl, from tlālli (“ground”) + coyōtl (“coyote”).

parole.significato: hardware dealer, the owner or employee of a tlapalería (hardware store or paint store)
parole.testo: From Classical Nahuatl tlapalli (“dye, ink, paint”) + -ero.

parole.significato: of, from or relating to the state of Tlaxcala, Mexico
parole.testo: Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tlaxcaltēcatl (“inhabitant of Tlaxcala”).
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tlahzolli (“trash, garbage, dirt”).
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tlecuilli.

Unknown; first attested in 1739. Attributed by folk etymology to the Latin bridal formula "Ubi tū Gāius ego Gāia" (literally “where you are Gaius, I am Gaia”). More likely a Mexican Spanish term from Classical Nahuatl tōcāyoh (“one who has a name, person of renown”), the possessive form of the noun
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl toloatzin.

parole.significato: a traditional musical instrument from northern Mexico, similar to a double bass
parole.testo: Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tololontic (“round”).
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tomatl (“tomatillo”), the tomato proper being xītomatl.
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tōtolin (“turkey hen”).

parole.significato: a baked corn tortilla, especially in the form of a chip or crisp; originating from Mexico
parole.testo: Clipping of totoposte, from Classical Nahuatl totopochtic (“something well toasted; toasted bread or tortilla”).

parole.significato: a field or marsh of tule reed
parole.testo: From Classical Nahuatl tōllin (“bulrush, sedge”).
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tōllin (“bulrush, sedge”).
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tzompantli.
From Classical Nahuatl xococ (“something sour”) + ātōlli (“atole”).

parole.significato: a species of prickly pear cactus, Opuntia matudae, native to Central Mexico
parole.testo: Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl xoconōchtli (“sour prickly pear”), from xococ (“something sour”) + nōchtli (“prickly pear”).

parole.significato: the youngest child of a family
parole.testo: Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl xōcōyotl (“youngest child”).
From Classical Nahuatl xoloitzcuintli (literally “dog of Xolotl”).
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl xoloitzcuintli (“Mexican hairless”).
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl xōlōitzcuintli.
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl xōchitl (“flower”).

parole.significato: a sweet tamale made with sweet corn, and is typically consumed with sour cream
parole.testo: Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl yelotamalli (“sweet corn tamale”), from yelotl (“sweet corn”) + tamalli (“something wrapped”).

parole.significato: a scourer made from plant fiber
parole.testo: Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl zacamecatl (“rope made with grass”), from zacatl (“grass”) + mecatl (“rope”).
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl zacatl (“dry weeds or grass; fodder, forage”), from Uto-Aztecan.
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl zacatecatl.
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl zacatōchin (literally “grass rabbit”), from Classical Nahuatl zacatl (“grass”) + tōchin, alternative form of tōchtli (“rabbit”).
From Classical Nahuatl Tzapotēcah, plural of Tzapotēcatl (“inhabitant of the place of sapote”).
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tzontli + pantli.

parole.significato: in some Mesoamerican civilizations, a wooden rack or palisade used for the public display of human skulls
parole.testo: Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tzompantli (“skull rack”), of debated composition. Perhaps from tzontli (“hair, head”) (compare tzontecomatl (“head, skull”)) + pantli (“flag, banner”), or simply (“row”).

parole.significato: A set of four hundred (especially of agricultural products)
parole.testo: Probably a reduction from Classical Nahuatl centzontli (“four hundred”).

parole.significato: a zopilote, a buzzard, a vulture
parole.testo: Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tzopīlōtl.

parole.significato: a type of palm tree (Brahea dulcis)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl zoyatl (“palm”).
Either from English shanty or Classical Nahuatl chāntli (“home”).
From Pipil chiltotl, from chiltik (“red”) + tutut (“bird”); or from Classical Nahuatl chīltōtōtl, from chīlli (“chili pepper”) + tōtōtl (“bird”).
